video_title: The Current State of Consumer AI
gist: a16z's Olivia Moore and Josh Elman unpack the 7th Top 100 consumer AI apps report, which adds Yipit card-spend data: only ~4.5% of US consumers pay for AI and spend is concentrated in power users of maker tools, while personal agents (Muse, Instinct) grow fast but remain niche. They argue consumer AI must shift from subscriptions to ads/transactions (OpenAI ads ~$1B run rate), note Claude passing Gemini in US paid subscribers, and map white space in 'spend time' and network categories.

themes.theme: Consumer AI is a power-user spend game

insights.claim: In a16z's 7th Top 100 consumer AI apps report, only 11 new products entered the web and mobile traffic lists combined, the fewest of any edition, suggesting traffic leadership is settling.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Traffic incumbency is consolidating; new entrants must win on spend/power users rather than broad traffic.
insights.quote: we only had 11 new products across the web and mobile list combined, which is the least we've had

insights.claim: When a16z added consumer card-spend data (via Yipit) for the first time, 29 of the 50 products ranking on spend did not appear on either traffic list, meaning traffic rankings badly miss where consumer AI money flows.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Screen consumer AI investments on paid-spend data, not traffic; many monetizing apps are invisible on traffic charts.
insights.quote: of those 50 that ranked for spend, 29 of them were not on either traffic list

insights.claim: About half of Americans report using AI and about 25% think they interact with AI near-daily, but only around 4.5% of US consumers pay for an AI subscription (some sources say 2-2.5%), roughly double a year ago.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Huge gap between usage and paying penetration defines both the upside and the monetization problem.
insights.quote: About half of Americans report using AI

insights.claim: Within the ~4.5% of US consumers who pay for AI, the top 10% of spenders generate more than half of revenue, the top 1% generate 20%, and the bottom 50% only about 16%.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Consumer AI revenue is extremely concentrated; churn of a small power-user cohort could swing revenues.
insights.quote: the top 1% are 20% of the revenue whereas the bottom 50% are like 16%

insights.claim: The median paying US consumer spends $25 per month on AI on personal cards, while the top 1% spends $93 per month (later referenced in conversation as $900 per month).
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: ARPU benchmarks for consumer AI; note internal inconsistency in the figure cited ($93 vs $900).
insights.quote: The top 1% user is spending $93 per month personally on their personal credit cards on AI.

insights.claim: Top consumer AI spenders over-index on build/make/sell tools: developer, productivity and creative products such as n8n, Granola, Higgsfield and Manus.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Highest willingness-to-pay sits with 'makers'; prosumer creation tools are the monetizable wedge.
insights.quote: it was mostly developer tools, um, productivity tools, creative tools, things used to like build, make, sell.

insights.claim: Josh Elman frames heavy personal AI spend as a harbinger of a new generation of 'makers' that will broaden as more people feel empowered to create, rather than a niche anomaly.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Bullish read: current power users are leading indicators of mainstream creation-tool demand.
insights.quote: I see these as harbingers of what's to come as more people feel empowered

insights.claim: The power-law concentration seen in consumer AI mirrors the enterprise side, per a16z's Sarah Wang commenting on the State of Markets report.
insights.speaker: Elena Burgerer
insights.so_what: Winner-take-most dynamics on both enterprise and consumer AI argue for concentrated bets on leaders.
insights.quote: there there's such a power law game happening now

themes.theme: Personal agents: fast growth, not yet mainstream

insights.claim: Personal/consumer agents are the biggest new consumer AI trend, emerging only in the last 3-4 weeks before the report, with very fast growth but not yet reaching mainstream users.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Early-stage category forming now; positions taken before next report edition may capture adoption inflection.
insights.quote: very very fast growth and yet still not quite reaching the mainstream user

insights.claim: OpenClaw, which would have ranked very high in the prior report, has disappeared from the rankings as its traffic completely declined after its team was acquired by OpenAI and it was overtaken by Grokbot, Town, OpenAI's Dots and others.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: First-mover agent products can collapse fast; category pioneers are not durable moats.
insights.quote: openclaw is nowhere in the rankings because the traffic has >> completely declined

insights.claim: OpenClaw marked a regime change around end of last year/early this year: AI shifted from a productivity tool to something that gets things done, triggering a run on Mac minis for running local agents.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Agentic use drives local compute/hardware demand and resets what consumers expect from AI.

insights.claim: Instinct announced 100,000 users growing 10% day over day, 40% of users connecting a credit card within three weeks, and over $1,000 average spend in the first month.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Transactional agents can drive large GMV per user quickly, pointing to take-rate business models.
insights.quote: they had announced like 40% of users connected a credit card in the first three weeks

insights.claim: Muse had about 500,000 downloads and 250,000 active users in its first ~12 days, but in US and Canada it reached about 5 million downloads versus Threads' ~16 million over the first ~22 days.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Even hit agent launches are ~3x smaller than social launches; mainstream pull remains limited.
insights.quote: In the first 22 days or so threads, it had about 16 million downloads and Muse is still sitting around 5 million.

insights.claim: Agent products like Muse are deliberately not growing aggressively because of a much higher cost to serve each user, unlike Threads, which needed rapid critical mass for network effects.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: High COGS throttles growth strategy; watch inference cost declines as the unlock for agent scale.
insights.quote: there's a much higher cost to serve these users. So they don't want it to get too big too fast.

insights.claim: Agent assistants gain platform-like compounding via app/merchant ecosystems, but it cuts both ways: Amazon blocks Muse from browsing and purchasing, while Muse has hundreds of partnerships such as Shopify.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Gatekeeping by Amazon vs openness of Shopify shapes which commerce platforms benefit from agentic shopping.
insights.quote: Amazon is like, "We're not going to allow Muse

insights.claim: No consumer assistant has yet unlocked person-to-person network effects, partly because the products know users so intimately that people resist bringing them into shared contexts.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Lack of network effects means agent lock-in must come from personal context, not social graphs.
insights.quote: I still don't feel like any of the assistant products have unlocked persontoperson network effects.

insights.claim: Trust, privacy and safety (an agent with email and credit-card access acting rogue or oversharing) is the biggest impediment to personal agents becoming massive consumer apps.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Trust/safety and permissioning infrastructure is a gating enabler for agent adoption.
insights.quote: that's going to be the biggest impingement on these things really growing is as massive consumer apps

insights.claim: Platform capabilities for agents are improving faster than genuine consumer willingness to use them.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Adoption lags capability; expect a delay between tech readiness and consumer revenue.
insights.quote: I think what the platforms are capable of is improving faster than true consumer willingness to use them.

insights.claim: Data from David Pollon's assistant benchmark (tracking 170-200+ agents, with a 1,500+ early-adopter community) shows coding and technical automation is still the #1 use of consumer assistants like Muse and Instinct, explaining reported costs of hundreds to thousands of dollars per user per month; mainstream-targeted agents see costs in the tens of dollars.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Headline agent cost-to-serve figures are skewed by power-user coding; mainstream unit economics are far better.
insights.quote: they're seeing costs in the tens of dollars, not the thousands of dollars a month

insights.claim: For non-technical users, agents feel like a 'blank box'; without social sharing of use cases (which drove social media diffusion), mainstream discovery of agent value is slow.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Products that productize use-case discovery or shareable outputs could crack mainstream agent adoption.
insights.quote: when you just hand this to somebody new it feels like a blank box

themes.theme: Business models: from subscriptions to ads and transactions

insights.claim: Olivia Moore, a self-described consumer AI maximalist, does not want the 4.5% paying-subscriber share to be the main growth path, arguing consumer AI must move to ads and transaction fees like prior consumer internet giants.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Upside in consumer AI may come from ad/transaction models, not subscription penetration.
insights.quote: We have transcended the need for everyone to buy a subscription to AI and we need to see these other business models come back.

insights.claim: In the Top 100 web list, about 85% of products monetize via subscriptions, 62% via credits or extra-usage payments, and only about 13% via ads or similar models, an inversion of consumer internet history.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Ad and transaction monetization in consumer AI is largely untapped white space.
insights.quote: Only like 13% had ads or other options where like you are the product

insights.claim: ChatGPT is already among the top 20 consumer subscription products globally after ~3.5 years, alongside mostly media companies and frequent-purchase platforms like Amazon and Uber.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: ChatGPT has reached media-scale subscription status at unprecedented speed.
insights.quote: Chachi BT is already on there which is crazy in like three and a half years of growth

insights.claim: High COGS has broken the classic consumer playbook of growing density at near-zero serving cost and monetizing later; AI startups must charge early and fear growing too fast without usage meters.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Consumer AI growth curves are capped by inference cost; falling inference cost is the key unlock for ad models.
insights.quote: that just isn't the case given how high COGS are

insights.claim: OpenAI reached roughly $1 billion annualized run rate in advertising as of August despite a slow partner-based rollout, a level that would previously take companies years after launching ads.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: OpenAI ads could become a major revenue line rapidly, threatening incumbent ad platforms.
insights.quote: they're already at, you know, a billion billion in annualized run rate

insights.claim: ChatGPT has about 1.2 billion weekly active users, providing ad density, and should command higher ad prices and conversion because it knows more about users; Login with ChatGPT and an upcoming wallet could further juice ads.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Signals ChatGPT evolving into an ad + identity + payments platform competing with Meta and Google.
insights.quote: chatbt has launched things like login with chatbt. I think a wallet is coming

insights.claim: OpenAI may achieve better ad targeting than Meta, previously best in class, because users have live, detailed conversations with ChatGPT.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Potential share shift in performance advertising from Meta toward OpenAI.
insights.quote: OpenAI uh being able to do crazy good targeting uh on consu like even better than I think Meta

insights.claim: Shift of chatbot queries toward shopping, advice and discovery creates commercial intent suitable for ads, but ads must be done deftly to avoid eroding trust in a personal product.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Commercial-intent queries migrating from Google search to chat is a structural ad-share risk for search.

insights.claim: Vertical consumer/prosumer AI products with dense valuable audiences can monetize via ads; OpenEvidence has 50-60% of US physicians on its product and has seen early ad success.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Vertical AI with professional audience density is a strong ad-monetization model.
insights.quote: 50 to 60% density of US all of all US physicians on the product

themes.theme: Lab battle: ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini

insights.claim: ChatGPT remains the dominant consumer AI by usage and revenue, about 6x Claude and about 2x Gemini on web traffic, with roughly 3x more US paid consumer subscribers than either Gemini or Claude.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: OpenAI's consumer lead is durable; competition is for second place.
insights.quote: chatbt is now ahead of Claude um around 6x on the web, around 2x uh ahead of Gemini on the web

insights.claim: Claude has passed Gemini in number of US paid consumer subscribers despite Gemini's far larger install base and Google distribution, driven by product launches like Claude Design and press since the Department of War episode in February.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Anthropic's consumer monetization is outperforming Google's distribution advantage.
insights.quote: Claude has actually passed Gemini in terms of number of paid subscribers

insights.claim: About 7.5% of Claude subscribers are on $100+/month Max plans versus about 1% for ChatGPT and Gemini, reflecting Anthropic's no-ads, subscription-heavy strategy.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Anthropic's consumer ARPU skews far higher; its user base is power users.
insights.quote: They have around seven and a half% of subscribers on the $100 plus per month

themes.theme: Creative tools: where labs win and specialists survive

insights.claim: In audio modalities the labs have not prioritized, specialists ElevenLabs and Suno consistently rank near the top of both traffic and spend lists; Suno built a strong lead partly because labs avoid music IP headaches.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Modalities with IP/legal friction create defensible windows for specialists.
insights.quote: Sunno has been able to kind of run away with a really strong lead

insights.claim: OpenAI (Images 2.0) and Google (Nano Banana, Veo) have taken much of the casual consumer traffic from standalone image generators; Midjourney fell off traffic rankings entirely but reappears on revenue rankings because power users value its taste and tunability.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Standalone gen-media apps survive via premium power-user taste, not mass traffic.
insights.quote: Midjourney was fairly high on our first ever rankings. It has fallen off the traffic rankings completely

insights.claim: Chinese AI video companies have an advantage in video generation because they can train on any data, and video's complexity rewards more training data.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Chinese players may lead AI video; data/IP regime is a competitive variable.
insights.quote: Chinese companies that can train on any data and do uh, have a real advantage

insights.claim: Creative tools that are agent-friendly and agent-accessible will see increasing tailwinds, as powerful models now tool-call out to external creative services.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: API/agent-accessibility becomes a distribution channel for creative software.
insights.quote: creative tools that are agentfriendly uh, and agent accessible are going to increasingly see really compelling tailwinds

insights.claim: Anthropic never built an image or video diffusion model, yet Claude users produce images and video because its coding ability generates them.
insights.speaker: Elena Burgerer
insights.so_what: Coding capability substitutes for modality-specific models, blurring creative-tool competition.

themes.theme: Startups vs labs: the software layer and white space

insights.claim: Consumer AI companies are becoming enterprise companies far faster than before ('the great expansion'): Krea, Replit, ElevenLabs, Gamma, Wispr Flow and Granola get pulled into enterprises via PLG, whereas Canva took 6+ years to build team/enterprise revenue.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Work-adjacent prosumer AI tools have low-cost PLG paths to enterprise revenue.
insights.quote: Canva took six plus years to have real team and enterprise revenue

insights.claim: Incumbents are unwilling or unable to cannibalize existing interfaces: Google hasn't reinvented Docs, Gmail or Calendar for AI, and OpenAI and Anthropic have been much less successful with launches outside ChatGPT, Codex, Claude or Claude Code.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Leaves room for startups reinventing interfaces even against frontier labs.
insights.quote: incumbents being unwilling or unable to cannibalize their existing interfaces

insights.claim: Model improvements act as a rising tide: well-designed apps like Wispr Flow and Granola explode in utility when models improve, debunking the idea that only one or two companies can own the experience layer.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Application-layer startups gain operating leverage from model progress rather than being displaced.
insights.quote: to think that you know we only have one or two companies that can build that experience layer I think is what this sort of report sort of debunks

insights.claim: Plaud, an AI note-taker device with a subscription that started in China, made the revenue list; big labs like OpenAI will do hardware but move slower, leaving windows for startups.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: AI hardware + subscription is a monetizing startup niche while labs are slow.
insights.quote: OpenAI can and will do a hardware device but as we've seen with them it just everything takes longer

insights.claim: Josh Elman argues value is moving back to the software layer, with experience, network, context and community as the asset rather than the model; dismissive 'wrapper/harness' framing misreads rich products.
insights.speaker: Josh Elman
insights.so_what: Supports investing in AI application companies over assuming labs capture all value.
insights.quote: the value really now is moving back to the software layer

insights.claim: Town builds personal playbooks of a user's voice and context that are hard to migrate; an email 99.9% in your voice takes ~10 seconds to fix versus 10+ minutes at 85%, creating compounding personal lock-in.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Accumulated personal context is a real moat for agent/prosumer products.
insights.quote: the difference between an email that is 99.9% sounds like me and even an email that's 85% sounds like me

insights.claim: Most consumer AI so far is 'save time' (productivity, search replacement, editing); the biggest consumer companies historically are 'spend time' products (social, Netflix, TikTok, YouTube), which AI hasn't yet produced.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: The largest consumer AI outcomes likely remain unbuilt in entertainment/social.
insights.quote: most people aren't looking to save time. They're looking for ways to spend their time.

insights.claim: Network categories such as dating, recruiting and social AI have no AI-native winners on the list; marketplace categories like shopping and home buying remain open and may live inside agents or as AI-native marketplaces agents call.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: Clear white-space map for consumer AI venture bets.
insights.quote: there's no one on the list doing dating now

insights.claim: AI gaming and entertainment content isn't yet good enough for average viewers, with the exception of AI micro-dramas, which are blowing up.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore
insights.so_what: AI micro-dramas are an early breakout format in AI entertainment.
insights.quote: which maybe the exception of AI micro dramas, which are blowing up
